checks.claim: Key: in a mixture the iron keeps its magnetism, so a magnet swept over iron filings in sand pulls the iron out and leaves the sand
checks.note: Grokipedia: each component 'retains its inherent physical and chemical properties'; iron filings and sand separated 'by sweeping a magnet over the mixture'.

checks.claim: Wrong: iron and sand both cling (pale sand is mostly quartz, which a magnet does not pull)
checks.note: Quartz is diamagnetic ('weakly repelled by magnetic fields'), unsuitable for magnetic separation; sand is predominantly quartz (https://grokipedia.com/page/Sand). Naming the sand pale rightly steers away from magnetite-rich black sand.

checks.claim: Wrong: nothing clings because mixing changed the iron
checks.note: No chemical change in a mixture; the iron stays iron.

checks.claim: Wrong: nothing clings because the sand blocks the pull; context says sand does not stop the magnet reaching the iron
checks.note: Quartz is only weakly diamagnetic and does not shield a magnetic field; the classic demonstration (Grokipedia Mixture) works through the sand.

checks.claim: Key: a stack of sieves sorts grains by size
checks.note: Stack shaken 'to facilitate passage based on size'; sieves nested 'with the largest opening at the top'; used in 'geology for sediment analysis'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Their weight' (looked at hard: partly right?)
checks.note: Not partly right as the sorting rule. Sieves sort 'by size' on 'dimensional differences'; weight enters only afterwards, when each sieve's catch is weighed (Grokipedia Sieve, Sieve_analysis; https://byjus.com/chemistry/sieving : sieving cannot separate two substances of the same size). Size and weight correlate within one rock type, so a child may reason 'big = heavy', but a small dense grain still drops through; the context says exactly this. Keep.

checks.claim: Wrong: hardness; kind of rock
checks.note: A sieve cannot separate same-size grains of different rock or hardness.

checks.claim: Context: top sieve has the biggest holes; each catch is weighed afterwards
checks.note: 'Each sieve is weighed individually with its retained particles.'

checks.claim: Key: only the sand stays on the filter paper; dissolved salt passes through with the water
checks.note: RSC practical (ages 9-11 listed): 'the damp sand in the filter paper'; the filtrate is 'the salt solution'. Small caveat only: the damp sand holds a film of salt water, and salt beyond what the water can dissolve would also stay; neither makes 'Both' the intended or a defensible 5th-grade answer, since the stem has the salt stirred into a beaker of water.

checks.claim: Wrong: only the salt; nothing at all
checks.note: Solute particles 'pass through filters'; sand grains are held back.

checks.claim: Context: filter cannot take salt out of salt water; dry away the water to get it back
checks.note: RSC: 'Heat the salt solution gently' in an evaporating basin, then let the damp salt dry.

checks.claim: Key: after a month in a sealed flask, the blue is still spread evenly through the water; context says the dissolved bits never settle, however long it stands
checks.note: Solute particles in a solution are 'molecular or ionic in size and do not separate', 'do not settle'. True as stated for a sealed (no evaporation), pale, unsaturated solution. Only fringe exceptions exist (slow hydrolysis can deposit a trace of basic copper salt in some waters; a near-saturated solution that cools can crystallise), none of which makes a layer of colour; the stem's 'pale blue' and 'sealed' rule them out at this level.

checks.claim: Copper sulfate forms bright blue crystals and dissolves to a blue solution
checks.note: 'bright blue triclinic crystals or granules'; 'a blue solution of copper(II) sulfate'; highly soluble.

checks.claim: Wrong: settled layer at the bottom / risen layer at the top / gone and clear
checks.note: A solution keeps 'a uniform composition and appearance throughout'; suspensions separate on spinning or standing 'but not in solutions'.

checks.claim: Context: sand or mud in water settles
checks.note: Suspension particles 'settle out of the mixture upon standing due to gravity'.

checks.claim: Key: the last spoonful stays because the water holds all the salt it can (saturated)
checks.note: Saturated solution is the maximum solute dissolved, 'in dynamic equilibrium with any undissolved solute'.

checks.claim: Context number: about 36 g salt per 100 g water at room temperature
checks.note: '360 g per kg of water at 25 C, equivalent to 36 g per 100 g of water'; Grokipedia Solubility: 35.9 g/100 g at 20 C.

checks.claim: Wrong: last spoonful heavier; sank too fast; salt lost its power to dissolve
checks.note: None explains it; the limit is the water's capacity (more water would dissolve the same salt).

checks.claim: Key: the ice melts because salt water stays liquid at -5 C (freezing-point depression)
checks.note: Salt solutions 'exploit freezing-point depression to melt ice on pavements'; the depression grows with the amount of salt, down to about -21 C at saturation. Brine on a salted road is strong enough to stay liquid at -5 C.

checks.claim: Context: pure water freezes at 0 C, seawater at about -1.8 C
checks.note: NSIDC: fresh water 0 C; seawater near 32 PSU 'begins to freeze at -1.8C'.

checks.claim: Context logic: 'seawater freezes only at about -1.8 degrees. ... the salt water stays liquid at -5 degrees'
checks.note: Misleading as put side by side: seawater IS salt water, and at -5 C seawater-strength salt water (about 3.5 percent) would freeze. Water must hold about 8 percent salt (more than twice the sea's) to stay liquid at -5 C (table: 8 wt% freezes at -5.08 C; eutectic 23.3 wt% at -21.1 C). The missing step is 'the more salt, the colder it must get'. Fix: 'Pure water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius, and the more salt it holds, the colder it must be before it freezes: seawater freezes at about -1.8 degrees, and the strong salt water that road salt makes stays liquid far below -5.' Keep the rest.

checks.claim: Context: -5 C is within rock salt's working range (fact sheet: weak below about -9 C)
checks.note: Scientific American: salt solutions bring the freezing point down to about 15 F (-9.4 C); salt 'must be in a solution with liquid water'. Grokipedia Freezing-point depression: effectiveness 'diminishes below -9C'.

checks.claim: Wrong: salt gives off heat as it dissolves; context 'Dissolving salt gives off no heat'
checks.note: NaCl dissolution is 'slightly positive at approximately +3.9 kJ/mol, making the process endothermic'. Note: calcium chloride, also sold as a road de-icer, does give off heat as it dissolves (FHWA https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/publications/research/safety/95202/005.cfm). Optional tightening: say 'rock salt' in the stem so the heat lure is wrong for every reader.

checks.claim: Wrong: salt soaks the cold out of the ice; salt reacts with ice to make a new substance
checks.note: Freezing-point depression is a physical (colligative) effect; the slush is ice and salt water.

checks.claim: Key: the balance shows the same mass after the salt dissolves
checks.note: NGSS 5-PS1-2 / PS1.A: 'The amount (weight) of matter is conserved when it changes form, even in transitions in which it seems to vanish'; clarification names dissolving.

checks.claim: Context example: 150 g water + 10 g salt = 160 g salt water
checks.note: RSC worked answer: 150 g + 10 g salt = 160 g both when added and once it can no longer be seen (RSC's 150 g is 'beaker and water', but the context's arithmetic holds either way).

checks.claim: Wrong: a little less; a little more; only water and dish
checks.note: The 'less' and 'only water' lures are the documented misconception that solutes 'disappear'; none is true.

checks.claim: Key: freezing changes the water's volume but not its mass
checks.note: 'the mass of solid ice precisely equals the mass of resulting liquid water'; sealed bottle, so nothing escapes.

checks.claim: Context: water swells by about 9 percent as it freezes
checks.note: 'Upon freezing, water expands by about 9% in volume'; ice ~0.917 g/cm3 vs water 1 g/cm3.

checks.claim: Context: ice floats because it takes up more room for its mass, not because it weighs less than the water it came from
checks.note: Lower density (not lower mass) makes ice float.

checks.claim: Wrong: mass not volume; both; neither
checks.note: Mass is unchanged and volume grows, so each other pairing is wrong.

checks.claim: Key: rust is a new substance made from the iron
checks.note: 'iron atoms react with oxygen and water molecules to yield iron(III) oxide (rust)', a new material; a chemical change makes 'entirely new substances with different properties'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Iron and rainwater mixed together' (looked at hard: rust is hydrated, so is this partly right?)
checks.note: Rust is 'primarily hydrated iron(III) oxide (Fe2O3.nH2O)': water is bound into it and oxygen from the air is joined to the iron, so it is a compound, not a mixture of iron metal and water; no iron metal can be got back by drying. 'Mixed together' is wrong. The context avoids saying rust holds no water, and its 'helped by water' is a fair simplification (water is needed; dry iron does not rust).

checks.claim: Wrong: the same iron with a new colour; dried mud
checks.note: Rust has different properties from iron and is a product of the iron itself, not a deposit from outside.

checks.claim: Context: reddish-brown, crumbly, far weaker than iron; cannot be turned back into iron by drying or picking apart
checks.note: 'reddish-brown'; 'flaky, powdery, or scaly'; brittle, low tensile and compressive strength, little load-bearing capacity. The context limits irreversibility to drying or picking apart, which is correct (smelting can reduce iron oxide to iron, and the context does not deny that).

unit_notes: One error, in the road-salt context only (dda30a9702): it states seawater freezes at -1.8 C and then that salt water stays liquid at -5 C without saying that more salt means a lower freezing point; a one-clause fix is given. The four points flagged for a hard look were checked: 'Their weight' is not partly right for a sieve stack (size is the rule; weighing comes after); copper sulfate solution not settling is true as stated for a sealed, pale solution; the -5 C road and the heat lure are right for rock salt (calcium chloride does warm as it dissolves, so 'rock salt' in the stem would close that gap); rust as a new substance is fair to every wrong choice, including 'iron and rainwater mixed'. Grade notes (curriculum citations) were not web-checked; they are not shown to players.
